craft_claim: Rendering a subject as vast enough to exceed the narrator's existing frame produces awe; a sacred object described only in comfortable, already-mastered terms will not read as holy.

supporting_evidence.note: Keltner and Haidt define awe as an epistemic emotion triggered by perceived vastness and a need for accommodation, and list threat, beauty, ability, virtue, and the supernatural as colouring features.

supporting_evidence.location: The Idea of the Holy, chs. II-IV
supporting_evidence.note: Otto's numinous object is 'wholly other' and exceeds the categories of the experiencing subject, matching the accommodation criterion in a religious register.

counterevidence.note: Katz and Franz argue awe has no uncontested definition and that treating 'vastness' as necessary has neglected other awe experiences and cross-cultural variation.

scope: Descriptive craft guidance for passages whose object is meant to exceed the speaker; applies across narrative, essay, and devotional prose.
exceptions: Traditions that locate the sacred in domesticity or the everyday (e.g. Viraśaiva embodiment) may make smallness, not scale, the vehicle of awe.
